doc.title: Ray Drummond interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Why it is hard for a bassist to be a bandleader
summary: He explains that presenters now deal with agents, and that bassists are rarely accepted as leaders; he cites Mingus and Ellington/Hodges.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Yeah. Is it hard to be a band leader?

Well there are two parts to that answer. One yes, these days it’s more difficult to get gigs primarily because most people are represented. So unless you are represented, it’s not that you’re at a disadvantage it’s just that people who are the presenters are more used to now working with people, managers, agents, than musicians. I mean more and more now the business has become more institutionalized and so it’s not that the presenters don’t want to but the presenters have gotten used to working primarily with quote other professional people rather than the musicians themselves. I think they feel more comfortable, you know they have their own little cliques and all that sort of stuff you know. But that’s the first part of the answer. The second part is one that’s instrument specific. Bass players have not really been given much chance — they don’t get the same chances at becoming band leaders that trumpet players, saxophone players, drummers sometimes seem able to get what we call more play at becoming a leader. More opportunities to become a leader. Piano players are accepted as leaders immediately. That sort of thing. But it’s kind of — bass — we have always been in the background creating the heartbeats for groups that we perform with and so the bass player that steps out and says I’m the leader. Okay there’s another component to that though, and it has to do with the instrument itself. Because people don’t really, in one sense they don’t listen to the bass as a melodic instrument in the same way that a piano or trumpet or saxophone or trombone or baritone saxophone even — talk about instruments that are closer to the bass in terms of pitch. So what has happened is that we now seem to have to fight to become band leaders. Charles Mingus is a perfect example of someone who obviously was a band leader and yet he had to struggle and fight to be known. People still think of him primarily as a composer and a composer who with his band played primarily his compositions. Yet on the other hand you have the fact that he was obviously a leader. He obviously wanted to train other musicians, one. Because that’s in my opinion one of the functions of a leader is to actually serve as a training ground, the kinds of bands that leaders have, ones where you actually have musicians in your groups who are going to become leaders themselves go on to do whatever it is that they’re supposed to be doing. Although there are some exceptions to that. And of course like Duke Ellington for instance was not someone to particularly develop talent, but he could have, but because he was writing for those musicians individually many of them decided — look at Johnny Hodges for instances. Johnny Hodges was in and out of that band like a ping pong ball

because of the fact that Duke always would write these wonderful, wonderful venues for him, these wonderful pieces of music, and sure he could play it with his own group but it just didn’t have the same kind of impact for him I think. I think he just got a great feeling out of playing Duke’s music too. And so it’s like Duke made sure that you had enough money to survive so it’s kind of like why bite the hand that feeds me, that sort of thing, and that also nurtures you.
